notable_claims: System administrators have a responsibility to minimize subversion before it happens to prevent service disruption.
Reporting suspicious activity to the root administrator of a remote site is often the only reliable way to resolve security issues.
classification.summary: A discussion between system administrators regarding the ethics of reporting 'suspicious' user activity to other institutions. Wes Morgan argues that sysadmins have a professional obligation to be hypervigilant and intervene before a security breach occurs to protect their own users.

notable_claims: A USA Today article reported that over 75 women claimed to have been harassed in computer discussion groups.
classification.summary: Wes Morgan responds to a report in USA Today regarding freelance writer Stephanie Brail, who alleged she was sexually harassed by Usenet users. Morgan questions the distinction between offensive generalizations and legal harassment within public electronic forums. He invites individuals to provide examples of online harassment to better define where 'flamefests' cross into harassment.

notable_claims: A university cannot realistically guarantee a 'no sanctions' policy for public forum posts if a separate judicial system exists.
Responsibility for online expression should be placed on the user rather than managed by computing staff.
classification.summary: Wes Morgan critiques a draft computer system policy from an anonymous state university department. The original draft promised no sanctions for posting obscene or violent material; Morgan argues that users should instead be held responsible via the university's existing judicial system and legal frameworks.
